paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent can learn a useful starting policy from previously collected data, reducing the interactions needed when training continues online. The transition can nevertheless undo that advantage. Once the agent visits different states or chooses different actions, errors in its value estimates can grow through bootstrapping, where estimates are used to construct further learning targets.

This paper changes how the offline critic is prepared for online learning. Instead of directly transferring its state-action value function, the method post-processes that function to align it with the policy learned offline. This also restrains value estimates for actions outside that policy, addressing a source of trouble during the transition.

After this alignment, fine-tuning can proceed using standard actor-critic algorithms. The approach avoids the online distribution-divergence or density-ratio estimation required by the alternatives described in the abstract. Experiments on simulated robotic tasks report improved fine-tuned performance, supporting alignment as a practical way to preserve more of the benefit of offline preparation.
icml-2023-actor-critic-alignment-for-off.tldr: Aligning an offline critic with its learned policy improves subsequent online fine-tuning in simulated robotic tasks.

paragraphs: The paper studies classifiers that assign labels by thresholding a low-degree polynomial. Although an input has n attributes, the target classifier depends on only K of them. The challenge is to exploit that sparsity while learning from data containing adversarial corruption, rather than requiring a sample count that grows strongly with every available attribute.

The proposed algorithm works under a Gaussian input distribution and permits a fraction of examples to be corrupted through the nasty-noise model. For target error ε and polynomial degree d, its sample bound is O(K^(4d) ε^(-2d) log^(5d) n), with runtime (nd/ε)^O(d). The tolerated corruption fraction is at most O(ε^d). Thus, sample dependence on the total number of attributes is only polylogarithmic, although other dependencies remain substantial.

The method connects sparse input dependence to sparsity in a Chow vector expressed using Hermite polynomials. A robust estimator then either certifies an adequate approximation or identifies a polynomial filter for corrupted samples. This extends attribute-efficient robustness beyond the previously established special case of sparse homogeneous halfspaces.
icml-2023-attribute-efficient-pac-learni.tldr: A new algorithm learns sparse low-degree polynomial classifiers under Gaussian inputs with polylogarithmic sample dependence on input dimension despite bounded adversarial corruption.

paragraphs: Intrinsic rewards give reinforcement learning agents additional incentives to explore. The difficulty is making those incentives useful for the actual task: an exploration bonus can change what the agent is encouraged to optimize. This paper introduces AIRS, a method that adapts reward shaping during learning to provide exploration incentives while alleviating that biased-objective problem.

AIRS selects a shaping function from a predefined collection, using an estimate of task return available during training. Its central choice is therefore which available exploration incentive to apply as learning proceeds. Connecting that selection to estimated task performance makes the shaping mechanism responsive to the task, rather than leaving the same incentive fixed throughout training.

The work also supplies an intrinsic-reward toolkit with implementations of multiple approaches. The authors evaluate AIRS on tasks from MiniGrid, Procgen, and the DeepMind Control Suite. Their simulations show that AIRS can outperform the benchmark schemes with a simple architecture. These findings support adaptive selection among existing shaping functions as a useful mechanism for improving exploration.
icml-2023-automatic-intrinsic-reward-sha.tldr: AIRS adapts exploration rewards using estimated task return and outperforms benchmark schemes in simulation.

paragraphs: Formal differential privacy guarantees account for adversaries that can be stronger than practical attacks. Consequently, a trained model may offer better protection against a particular attack than its formal guarantee suggests. This paper studies empirical privacy estimation for specified threat models, using membership inference attacks that try to determine whether an example belonged to the training data.

Previous approaches build privacy-budget intervals from separate uncertainty intervals for an attack's false-positive and false-negative rates. Obtaining useful precision this way can require training many models. The proposed Bayesian method instead computes a joint posterior over those two error rates and transforms it into a posterior over the estimated privacy budget.

This produces a distribution over the privacy estimate and makes more efficient use of samples. The authors integrate it with membership inference attacks in an end-to-end system evaluated on text and vision classification. With the same sample count, reported intervals are up to 40% narrower than prior work. Those estimates describe protection against the specified attacks, rather than replacing the formal privacy guarantee.
icml-2023-bayesian-estimation-of-differe.tldr: Bayesian analysis of membership inference errors yields more sample-efficient privacy estimates for specific threat models.

paragraphs: Community detection often groups network nodes into blocks, but the interactions themselves may also belong to different categories. Those categories can have different community structures. A single grouping of nodes can therefore overlook distinctions that arise from the kinds of interactions taking place within a complex system.

CataBEEM models both hidden interaction categories and category-dependent node communities. It treats the network through the process that generates interactions and can incorporate prior knowledge from additional information attached to individual interactions. This gives the model a way to connect what kinds of exchanges occur with how participating nodes form communities.

The authors derive an efficient variational inference algorithm applicable to networks containing millions of interactions, along with a theoretical bound on the misspecification rate. Simulations and an application to TalkLife, an online peer-support network, demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The reported results include more temporally consistent communities and better predictions than other methods, supporting the value of modeling interaction categories alongside node groups.
icml-2023-catabeem-integrating-latent-in.tldr: CataBEEM jointly models interaction categories and node communities, improving reported community consistency and prediction.

paragraphs: Prediction intervals should communicate uncertainty, but missing input values complicate what their coverage guarantees mean. The paper shows that conformal prediction retains its overall coverage guarantee after imputation for any missingness distribution and almost all imputation functions. That average guarantee can still hide intervals that cover too rarely for particular patterns of missing inputs.

To address this mismatch, the authors introduce missing data augmentation within a generalized conformalized quantile regression framework. The resulting intervals are valid conditionally on the missingness pattern, despite the exponentially many possible patterns. This makes the guarantee sensitive to which information is unavailable, rather than relying solely on coverage averaged over all cases.

A further theoretical result connects universally consistent quantile regression on imputed data to Bayes-optimal pinball risk and coverage conditional on a given data point. A linear-model analysis shows why missing values can create varying uncertainty across examples. Experiments with synthetic and critical-care data support the theory and report improved performance for the proposed methods.
icml-2023-conformal-prediction-with-miss.tldr: Missing data augmentation provides conformal intervals valid for individual missingness patterns, addressing gaps hidden by overall coverage.

paragraphs: This paper studies objectives written as a ratio. The numerator combines a differentiable convex function with a potentially nonsmooth convex function, while the denominator may be convex or concave. Despite that structure, the overall optimization problem is nonconvex, so familiar guarantees for convex minimization do not automatically apply.

The authors propose two coordinate descent methods that globally solve a one-dimensional subproblem at each iteration. Both converge to coordinate-wise stationary points. For a convex denominator, a weak local bounded-nonconvexity condition makes this stationarity notion stronger than the standard critical-point and directional-point notions considered in the paper. Additional suitable conditions yield Q-linear convergence to such points.

The concave-denominator case gives a stronger conclusion: every critical point is a global minimum, and the methods reach a global minimum at a sublinear rate. These distinctions explain why denominator structure matters for what the algorithms can guarantee. Applications to machine learning and signal processing, with experiments on real-world data, report significant and consistent accuracy improvements over existing methods.
icml-2023-coordinate-descent-methods-for.tldr: Two coordinate descent methods exploit ratio-objective structure to obtain convergence guarantees that depend on the denominator and additional conditions.

paragraphs: Some theories explain neural-network regression by assuming inputs lie exactly on a low-dimensional manifold. This paper relaxes that requirement: inputs need only concentrate around a subset of the surrounding space. It introduces effective Minkowski dimension to describe the complexity of that subset and connect concentrated data geometry to learning difficulty.

Under the proposed setting, the authors prove that sample complexity depends on this effective dimension. Their example uses a Gaussian input distribution with a full-rank covariance matrix, so the data need not occupy an exactly lower-dimensional manifold. What matters is how quickly the covariance eigenvalues decrease, indicating how unevenly variation is distributed across directions.

For exponential eigenvalue decay, the effective dimension grows as O(√log n); for polynomial decay, it grows as O(n^γ), where γ is a small positive constant determined by the decay rate. Here n is the sample size. The theory therefore explains how deep regression can adapt to concentrated, full-dimensional data and avoid the curse of ambient dimensionality at moderate sample sizes.
icml-2023-effective-minkowski-dimension-.tldr: Effective Minkowski dimension explains how deep regression can exploit concentrated data without requiring an exact low-dimensional manifold.

paragraphs: Dictionary learning represents data using a shared collection of basic components, or atoms. Applying this idea to graphs is difficult because different graphs can inhabit different metric spaces. Existing graph dictionary methods described in the paper emphasize reconstruction and often produce linear embeddings at substantial computational cost.

The authors introduce FraMe, a mixture model based on Fused Gromov-Wasserstein distance, to approach dictionary learning through graph generation. Its graph-generation function combines that distance with a radial basis function kernel. This construction creates nonlinear embedding spaces, and the paper proves that those spaces provide a good approximation to the original graph spaces.

FraMe also includes a fast solution built on expectation-maximization, with a convergence guarantee. The theoretical approximation result addresses the quality of the representation space, while the algorithm addresses how to fit the model. Experiments evaluate both node and graph embeddings and report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods, supporting the usefulness of the generative formulation for representing graph data.
icml-2023-generative-graph-dictionary-le.tldr: FraMe uses a generative mixture model to learn nonlinear graph representations with theoretical approximation and convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning produces node representations and has attracted broad interest, but this paper examines its exposure to malicious backdoors. The authors study security across a pipeline that can involve republishing both data and models. This broader view matters because vulnerabilities can arise at different stages of the learning process.

The proposed GCBA framework includes three attacks: poisoning, crafting, and natural backdoor, each aimed at one pipeline stage. The authors formulate these attacks as optimization problems. Because graph data involve discrete structures, they introduce a discrete optimization technique to solve the resulting problems rather than treating graph changes as ordinary continuous adjustments.

Evaluations across multiple datasets and graph contrastive learning methods report high attack success rates while preserving stealthiness. The paper also examines potential countermeasures and finds the existing defenses considered insufficient to mitigate GCBA. These results identify backdoors as a practical vulnerability in the evaluated settings and motivate defenses designed specifically for graph contrastive learning and its data-and-model reuse process.
icml-2023-graph-contrastive-backdoor-att.tldr: GCBA demonstrates stealthy backdoor vulnerabilities across graph contrastive learning stages that the evaluated defenses fail to adequately mitigate.

paragraphs: Exact dot-product attention requires time and memory that grow quadratically with sequence length. KDEformer targets two expensive operations: computing the normalization terms in softmax and multiplying the resulting attention matrix by the values. Reducing these costs makes attention more manageable as the number of sequence elements increases.

The key observation is that softmax normalization can be expressed as a variant of kernel density estimation. An efficient solver for that problem also helps accelerate the matrix product through subsampling. The resulting approximation runs in subquadratic time and comes with spectral-norm error bounds, which characterize matrix-level error rather than bounding individual entries alone.

Experiments on pretrained models report improvements over other attention approximations in accuracy, memory use, and arithmetic operations. For BigGAN image generation, the authors report better generative scores than exact computation with more than fourfold speedup. For T2T-ViT ImageNet classification, they report more than eighteenfold speedup with less than a 0.5% accuracy drop. These results demonstrate favorable efficiency-quality trade-offs in the evaluated applications.
icml-2023-kdeformer-accelerating-transfo.tldr: KDEformer approximates attention through kernel density estimation and subsampling, combining subquadratic computation with matrix-level error guarantees.

paragraphs: A representation learned for one task and distribution may omit features that become useful elsewhere. This paper argues that preparing for changing tasks or distributions calls for richer representations than a single training run tends to produce. It supports that argument with simple theory and an experiment based on combining independently learned features.

The authors train networks using identical data, models, algorithms, and hyperparameters, changing only the random seed. They then concatenate the resulting representations. Although the individual networks perform similarly, their combined representation substantially outperforms an equivalently sized network trained once in a number of scenarios involving new distributions.

The findings show that similar training performance can conceal meaningful differences in learned representations. Features from separate runs add little information for the original task under its original distribution, yet can become much more informative after a shift. The proposed explanation is that one optimization run has little incentive to collect features that do not incrementally improve its training objective, even if those features could help later.
icml-2023-learning-useful-representation.tldr: Combining representations from different random-seed training runs improves transfer in several settings where tasks or distributions change.

paragraphs: CPUs can be attractive for model inference because of workflow, security, and cost considerations, but their compute capabilities differ sharply from GPUs. This paper focuses on feed-forward networks built around general matrix multiplication, a common component of modern neural architectures, and asks how much of their arithmetic can be removed.

LookupFFN reformulates these networks so that most essential operations become memory lookups. The design draws inspiration from locality-sensitive hashing approaches to approximating feed-forward networks. Its central trade-off is to use memory resources to reduce computation, matching the paper's motivation of making inference less demanding on CPU arithmetic capabilities.

In RoBERTa language-model pretraining, the proposed formulation achieves performance similar to matrix-multiplication-based feed-forward networks while dramatically lowering the required floating-point operations. The authors also profile hardware strategies intended to maximize efficiency on contemporary and anticipated hardware. Together, the formulation and profiling connect an algorithmic reduction in arithmetic with the practical question of how a lookup-based design can make effective use of hardware resources.
icml-2023-lookupffn-making-transformers-.tldr: LookupFFN replaces much feed-forward-network arithmetic with memory lookups, maintaining similar RoBERTa pretraining performance with far fewer floating-point operations.

paragraphs: Speech recognition systems face two connected challenges: adding languages without excessive overhead and adapting to languages with little training data. Low-resource adaptation also raises concerns about overfitting and forgetting previously learned knowledge. Master-ASR addresses these challenges through a modular architecture built around components shared across languages.

The framework first learns a small collection of generalizable submodules, then adaptively assembles them for different languages. Sharing those components is intended to reduce multilingual training, inference, and storage burdens while enabling knowledge transfer during adaptation. Experiments and visualizations indicate that the framework can discover similarities among languages through this approach.

For multilingual recognition, the authors report character error rates lower by 0.13–2.41 and 30% smaller inference overhead than state-of-the-art solutions. For low-resource tuning, they report comparable character error rates with nearly 100 times fewer trainable parameters. These results support modular sharing as a way to improve the balance between recognition quality and the resources required to support or adapt to additional languages.
icml-2023-master-asr-achieving-multiling.tldr: Master-ASR shares and assembles language modules to improve multilingual recognition efficiency and enable parameter-efficient low-resource adaptation.

paragraphs: Individual fairness asks an algorithm to treat similar individuals similarly. Matrix estimation addresses another problem: recovering useful information from data containing noise and missing values. This paper connects the two by asking whether improving the data before prediction can also improve an algorithm's individual fairness.

The proposed preprocessing step uses singular value thresholding, a matrix estimation method. Under appropriate conditions, the authors prove that this step provides a strong individual-fairness guarantee. Fairness is therefore addressed through the data supplied to a base algorithm, with the theoretical result explaining when that intervention can improve the similarity of treatment.

Under analogous conditions, the estimates are also consistent and approximately minimax optimal, meaning they have strong statistical accuracy properties. The paper concludes that, under its stated conditions, preprocessing does not increase the base algorithm's prediction error and therefore does not impose a fairness-performance trade-off. Experiments on synthetic and real data support these results. The conditional guarantees are central: they establish circumstances in which fairness and predictive performance can improve together.
icml-2023-matrix-estimation-for-individu.tldr: Under suitable conditions, singular value thresholding improves individual fairness without increasing prediction error.

paragraphs: Iterative machine teaching studies how a teacher can supply examples over time to help a learner reach a target model quickly. Existing approaches focus on parameterized model families and measure progress in parameter space. That focus becomes awkward when the desired target is specified directly as a function rather than through a parameter vector.

This paper formulates nonparametric iterative machine teaching as optimization in function space. It proposes both random and greedy functional teaching algorithms. The change of viewpoint allows the teaching objective to concern the function the learner should acquire, extending the setting beyond the parameter-based formulation used by earlier methods.

The theory analyzes iterative teaching dimension, a measure of the teaching effort required. Under appropriate assumptions, the random algorithm gives a uniform upper bound for the nonparametric setting. The greedy algorithm has a significantly lower teaching dimension and yields a tighter bound. Experiments in nonparametric scenarios support the theoretical findings, linking the broader formulation to a measurable advantage from choosing teaching examples greedily.
icml-2023-nonparametric-iterative-machin.tldr: A function-space formulation extends iterative machine teaching to nonparametric targets and gives greedy teaching tighter effort bounds than random teaching.

paragraphs: Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning aims to learn stable joint behavior from previously collected game data. This paper provides a unified framework for approximating Nash, correlated, and coarse correlated equilibria in Markov games. It accommodates general function approximation, extending beyond the tabular and linear models emphasized in earlier work.

The framework uses Bellman-consistent pessimism to construct intervals for policy returns. Both ends of those intervals help form a relaxed measure of a candidate policy's equilibrium gap, which becomes the optimization objective. This turns uncertainty about returns into a quantity the learning procedure can use when comparing candidate solutions.

The guarantees require data coverage, but the proposed condition improves on unilateral concentrability. It permits selective coverage of deviation policies that balance being close to best responses with being supported by the available data. The authors identify scenarios where this gives substantially better guarantees. They also show that the framework encompasses apparently different solution concepts for two-player zero-sum games, connecting those special cases to the broader treatment.
icml-2023-offline-learning-in-markov-gam.tldr: A unified offline Markov-game framework learns three equilibrium types with general function approximation under an improved data-coverage condition.

paragraphs: A learned index predicts where an item is located in an array, helping answer queries about matching elements. Such indexes have shown large empirical speed advantages over conventional methods, but the theory described in this paper had previously established only logarithmic query time, alongside a constant-factor space improvement under distributional assumptions.

The authors prove a stronger result: under mild assumptions on the data distribution, a learned index can achieve O(log log n) expected query time while using the same asymptotic space complexity as non-learned methods. Here n is the array size. The result improves the growth rate of expected query cost, rather than merely changing a constant factor.

A second result permits slightly greater, but still near-linear, space use and obtains O(1) expected query time. Together, these guarantees provide a theoretical explanation for substantial learned-index speedups and show how extra storage can change the attainable query complexity. The claims are distribution-dependent and concern expected time, preserving the distinction between these guarantees and an unrestricted worst-case promise.
icml-2023-on-distribution-dependent-sub-.tldr: Under distributional assumptions, learned indexes achieve doubly logarithmic expected query time, or constant expected time with slightly more space.

paragraphs: This paper asks what a foundation model could accomplish even if data, computation, model size, training quality, and pretext-task generalization were ideal. Removing those familiar obstacles isolates a different question: whether success on the pretext task supplies the right structure for a downstream task. The authors use category theory to investigate that question.

Their first result characterizes prompt-based learning: a downstream task can be solved through prompts if and only if it is representable in the framework. Their second result shows that fine-tuning does not face this same limit. With enough resources, a foundation model possessing the minimum required power, up to symmetry, can theoretically solve tasks within the category defined by the pretext task.

A third theorem shows how structural information from a source category can enable generation of unseen objects in a target category, such as generating images using text structure. The paper also develops a categorical framework for supervised and self-supervised learning. These are theoretical statements within an idealized setup, distinguishing structural capability from practical training success.
icml-2023-on-the-power-of-foundation-mod.tldr: Category theory characterizes prompting limits, fine-tuning capability, and cross-category generation for idealized foundation models.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search methods are often compared using the DARTS search space. This paper examines a weakness of that benchmark: its architectures can occupy a narrow accuracy range, making method rankings less informative. The authors observe that this issue already affects some studies and reduces the meaning of their reported scores.

They introduce LHD, a larger and harder search space assembled through a suite of improvements while retaining efficient search. The benchmark built around it aims to make differences between methods easier to distinguish without making evaluation inaccessible. This connects benchmark design to the practical question of whether scores reveal meaningful differences in search quality.

The authors reimplement twelve baselines and evaluate them across twelve conditions combining transductive robustness and discretization policy, two influential factors they identify as underexplored. The resulting comparison examines methods under multiple conditions rather than relying on a single score. The contribution is an expanded evaluation foundation intended to support future architecture-search research and address shortcomings the authors identify in tabular benchmarks.
icml-2023-rethink-darts-search-space-and.tldr: LHD expands the DARTS search space and evaluates twelve baselines across twelve conditions to make architecture-search comparisons more informative.

paragraphs: Counterfactual risk minimization learns an improved decision policy from logged bandit feedback: records generated by a previous policy with feedback on its chosen actions. This paper considers a setting where learning need not stop after one offline update. A learned policy can be deployed, collect additional data, and support another round of improvement.

The authors extend the framework and its theory to this repeated-deployment setting, calling it sequential counterfactual risk minimization. They introduce a new counterfactual estimator and analyze how using successive deployments can improve learning. Their analysis draws on ideas resembling restart strategies in accelerated optimization, connecting repeated policy updates to improved theoretical rates.

The paper identifies conditions under which excess-risk and regret rates improve over CRM. Those conditions are part of the claim: repeated deployment is analyzed as an opportunity for improvement, rather than asserted to help unconditionally. Empirical evaluations with both discrete and continuous actions demonstrate benefits from multiple CRM deployments, supporting the value of treating data collection and policy improvement as a sequence.
icml-2023-sequential-counterfactual-risk.tldr: Sequential counterfactual risk minimization uses repeated policy deployments and fresh data to improve learning rates under identified conditions.

paragraphs: The authors track attention entropy during Transformer training, measuring how concentrated each attention head's scores become. Across architectures and tasks, they observe that pathologically low entropy accompanies unstable training, including oscillating loss and divergence. They call this concentration entropy collapse and use it to guide a stabilization method.

Their method, σReparam, reparameterizes every linear layer using spectral normalization and an additional learned scalar. Experiments show that it prevents attention entropy collapse and promotes stability. A theoretical lower bound supplies further motivation: the bound on attention entropy decreases exponentially with the spectral norm of attention logits, linking the scale of those logits to possible attention concentration.

Evaluations span image classification, image self-supervised learning, translation, speech recognition, and language modeling. The method improves robustness to hyperparameter choices. Reported examples include competitive Vision Transformer training without warmup, weight decay, layer normalization, or adaptive optimizers, and competitive speech recognition without warmup or adaptive optimizers. These findings show that controlling this aspect of the network can reduce reliance on several usual training aids in the tested settings.
icml-2023-stabilizing-transformer-traini.tldr: σReparam uses spectral normalization and learned scaling to prevent attention entropy collapse and stabilize Transformer training.

paragraphs: Autoregressive language models generate text successfully, but imposing constraints introduces a difficult probabilistic problem. Even simple requirements about which words appear make sampling from the model's distribution conditional on those requirements intractable. The challenge is therefore more than producing fluent continuations: generation must account for conditions on the resulting text.

GeLaTo combines autoregressive generation with tractable probabilistic models, which permit efficient calculations involving lexical constraints. The paper demonstrates this using distilled hidden Markov models to guide generation from GPT2. The tractable model provides a place to compute the constrained probabilities efficiently, making those calculations available to steer the language model's output.

On challenging constrained-generation benchmarks, including CommonGen, GeLaTo achieves state-of-the-art performance and exceeds strong baselines by a large margin. The results support combining language generation with a separate probabilistic model whose structure makes constraint calculations manageable. The authors also identify more expressive tractable models as a promising direction, since this framework connects the ability to represent language with the ability to reason efficiently about constraints.
icml-2023-tractable-control-for-autoregr.tldr: GeLaTo uses tractable probabilistic models to guide GPT2 toward lexical constraints, achieving strong constrained-generation benchmark results.

paragraphs: Combining several neural networks can improve predictions, but running every ensemble member makes inference expensive. Work on mode connectivity shows that different trained parameter settings can be linked by low-loss subspaces, allowing ensemble members to be collected efficiently. That training advantage still leaves the cost of separate forward passes at prediction time.

This paper introduces a lightweight bridge network to reduce that cost. Given a low-loss subspace connecting two network modes, the bridge predicts what the original network would output at a selected point in that subspace. It uses a small amount of features from the original network instead of requiring another full forward pass for that prediction.

The approach moves some ensemble computation into a cheaper output-prediction problem. Its starting point is an available low-loss connection, which supplies the network behaviors the bridge should approximate. Experiments show that these bridge networks can be trained and can significantly reduce inference costs. The contribution therefore addresses the deployment bottleneck that remains even when obtaining ensemble parameters is efficient.
icml-2023-traversing-between-modes-in-fu.tldr: Lightweight bridge networks predict outputs along low-loss parameter subspaces, reducing the full-network evaluations needed for ensembling.

paragraphs: Off-policy reinforcement learning uses data generated by behavior different from the policy being evaluated. With function approximation, theory often assumes Bellman completeness: the function class remains compatible with Bellman updates. This paper studies the weaker structural assumption of realizability, asking what guarantees remain when the class can represent the target but may lack that closure property.

The authors establish finite-sample guarantees without an inherent Bellman-error approximation term. The bounds depend on three interacting quantities: the function class's metric entropy, a concentrability coefficient measuring the cost of off-policy learning, and a new measure of misalignment between the class and its image under the Bellman operator.

That third quantity records how Bellman completeness is violated, allowing the analysis to reflect degrees of mismatch rather than demanding completeness outright. The results therefore clarify how representation complexity, off-policy coverage, and structural alignment jointly influence statistical difficulty. The analysis also applies directly to solutions reached by temporal-difference algorithms when they converge; it does not itself assert that those algorithms always converge.
icml-2023-when-is-realizability-sufficie.tldr: Off-policy learning guarantees under realizability depend on function-class complexity, data coverage, and a new measure of Bellman misalignment.
